title: Inference Debug Lab: Console Forensics & Error Path Walkthrough - OrbitMed
next_steps: Redwood to share private deployment security pack link
SE to provision sample trace ingestion template
action_items: Priya Desai: Prepare sample trace ingestion template by 2026-09-02
Jordan Lee: Send pricing and dedicated capacity options doc by 2026-09-01
OrbitMed (Ruth): Provide a 24-hour request log extract for pilot by 2026-09-03
summary: Redwood SE walked OrbitMed through the Console's trace-forensics workflow: how request logs, request playback, and trace correlator help reproduce and root-cause intermittent inference errors. Discussed KV cache fallbacks, model variant routing, and security/compliance needs for a pilot. Agreed next steps to run a short benchmark pilot and exchange security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, account exec at Redwood. Today Priya and Marco will run through a live debug lab on the Console. Ruth, Samir, Emily, Kenji, you good with agenda?
[00:08] Ruth Alvarez: Yes thanks Jordan, excited. We're seeing occasional 500-like errors when routing to model v2-stable, and it's causing retries in our pipelines.
[00:18] Priya Desai: Okay great, that's exactly the kind of thing the trace inspector was built for. We'll show how to find the failed request, replay it, and examine KV cache and fallback behavior. Quick callout, transcription might flip some acronyms — KV sometimes comes out as "K-V" or "K V" in auto captions.
[00:33] Emily Wong: Sounds good. Our SRE noticed spikes at 3am UTC and again midday US. We suspect a cache eviction.
[00:40] Samir Patel: Yeah — perf looks fine by averages but tail latency jumps and then consumers see errors. We want to prove whether it's a runtime bug or configuration.
[00:49] Priya Desai: Cool. I'll share my screen. (screen-share) Alright, console home — hop into the Trace Inspector. I have a filter set for OrbitMed-prod, model: v2-stable, timeframe: past 72 hours.
[01:08] Jordan Lee: Priya, quick question for context — are you simulating a dedicated node or hosted? OrbitMed currently on hosted plan, right?
[01:15] Ruth Alvarez: Correct hosted. We're evaluating dedicated/reserved for predictable latency.
[01:19] Marco Chen: We should cover both paths today: hosted fallback behavior and what changes under Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) since the fallback rules differ slightly.
[01:27] [02:05] Priya Desai: Alright, here's a failed request. HTTP status 500 at the serving gateway, and trace shows a model load timeout at the runtime layer — you'll see the stack frame mapping to the runtime shard. Timestamp here 03:12:42 UTC.
[02:22] Priya Desai: Notice the request trace contains the request headers, model selection decision, and a per-hop latency heatmap. The heatmap shows a big spike at the 'model loading' step.
[02:36] Samir Patel: That's interesting — our logs show an earlier error, maybe the orchestration retried and then evicted KV. Could be related.
[02:45] Priya Desai: Let's jump to Request Playback. This will reconstruct the same inference call including prompt, tokenization, and KV cache references. Playback uses the stored KV snapshot if available, otherwise it'll indicate a cache-miss.
[03:05] Ruth Alvarez: Playback — does that mean it actually runs a mini-inference against the same model binary?
[03:10] Priya Desai: It replays through a sandboxed runtime path that reproduces runtime behavior without incurring production quotas — we snapshot the inputs and request metadata. If KV snapshot is missing, the log will show 'kv:MISS' and then the fallthrough behavior.
[03:25] [05:12] Priya Desai: Here's the replay result: got a 500 on step 'model load' again. In the expanded view you can see 'kv:MISS' followed by a 'fallback:model-quant' route. That matches your observed retries hitting a quantized variant which in this case didn't have enough warmed-up shards.
[03:44] Samir Patel: So the system automatically routes to a quantized variant if the primary variant isn't available? We didn't expect that — our app assumes strict model pinning.
[03:52] Marco Chen: Good catch. By default the routing policy is 'performance-first' with soft fallbacks. You can pin via the rollout rules to disallow automatic substitute variants; we'll show that config and also how to create a canary that prevents silent fallbacks.
[04:06] Emily Wong: That may explain why the output changed sometimes too. When fallback happens, semantics can shift slightly.
[04:14] Priya Desai: Exactly — that's why the console also surfaces 'semantic drift' flags when the output token distribution diverges beyond a threshold in the replay.
[04:21] [07:00] Priya Desai: Switching to the correlation view: you can correlate trace IDs across the request ingest, runtime logs, and infra metrics. See the correlation panel linking the trace ID to the GPU memory pressure spike on host-15.
[04:42] Ruth Alvarez: Host-15 — we can look at historical eviction patterns for that host. Samir, do you have host names in your fleet?
[04:49] Samir Patel: Yes, we do. We'll cross-ref.
[04:52] Priya Desai: Note the console also shows a compacted event list: model load, kv-evict, kernel OOM, fallback. The sequence suggests the model loader couldn't allocate the KV snapshot after a kernel reclamation.
[05:08] [09:20] Jordan Lee: Quick break for security question — Kenji, do you want us to pause on any PCI/HIPAA related items?
[05:15] Kenji Ito: Yes — can you confirm whether request payload is persisted for playback in hosted? We need to ensure PHI is masked or the data residency rules are honored.
[05:25] Priya Desai: Great question. For hosted playback we store an encrypted snapshot in an isolated tenancy with customer-scoped keys; we also support retention controls and redaction hooks. We'll share the whitepaper: https://redwood-inference.com/security-pilot-pack. For private deployments, snapshots stay in your VPC and are controlled by your KMS.
[05:40] Kenji Ito: Okay, can you send the SOC2/ISO certs and the redacted retention policy?
[05:45] Jordan Lee: We'll send the security pack and SOC2 link right after this call. That's one of the next steps.
[05:50] [12:10] Priya Desai: Back to the trace: here's a useful trick — you can open a collapsed span and click 'Show related logs' which surfaces the raw request log line and any Docker/K8s container logs we ingested. See log line: 'Runtime: shard 3 oom reclaim -> evict kv snapshot id 0x4f2a'.
[06:14] Samir Patel: That log line rings true with an eviction policy we saw. Does Redwood ingest K8s evictions from host kubelet?
[06:21] Priya Desai: Yes we support node-level event ingestion (kubelet events, host metrics) if you flip the agent on. For private deployments, you push via our telemetry forwarder; for hosted, we pull from integrated cloud logs with consent.
[06:36] [15:00] Priya Desai: Now, reproducing the error locally: you can export the request payload via 'Export for debugging' — it gives you a tarball with prompt, token slices, and the KV reference. We provide helper scripts to simulate the KV miss.
[06:58] Ruth Alvarez: That would be super useful. We'll need to run the simulation in our staging cluster.
[07:05] Priya Desai: I'll attach the export template as part of the action items.
[07:12] Marco Chen: Also, for the pilot we'd recommend enabling 'prefix caching' and bumping the KV retention for hot routes; that reduces cold-starts and avoids repeated load timeouts. There is a unit-cost tradeoff we can optimize in Redwood Optimize.
[07:26] [18:21] Samir Patel: Can you quantify the cost hit for longer KV retention? Ballpark — like 10% more tokens or 5% GPU time?
[07:35] Marco Chen: It depends on workload shape. For chat-like workloads with long context it's more GPU-mem vs compute. Ballpark: retaining hot-kv for the top 5% of prefixes might increase memory by ~8-12% but reduce load events by ~60-80% which nets out to lower overall cost. We'll provide a simulation for your logs.
[07:58] Priya Desai: Also worth mentioning: Dedicated pools give you warmed-up model residency which almost eliminates model load timeouts, so the operational variance drops dramatically.
[08:10] [21:00] Emily Wong: If we move to Dedicated, are we able to keep private telemetry in our VPC? Compliance wants flow logs+audit trail inside our network.
[08:17] Jordan Lee: Yes, Private deployment (VPC/on-prem) offers customer-managed control plane; audit logs and telemetry can be stored in your S3/Blob and keyed with your KMS.
[08:26] Kenji Ito: Great. We'll want to run a small on-prem-like pilot to validate that retention and KMS flow.
[08:32] [24:45] Priya Desai: Switching gears — let's run a handcrafted failure path. I'm going to force a simulated kv-evict and repro. (pauses) Replaying — there, console shows a diff view: primary output vs quantized fallback, token mismatch flagged.
[08:55] Ruth Alvarez: That token mismatch is exactly what caused downstream classifier failures in our pipeline. Important to detect.
[09:02] Priya Desai: You can set a regression alert on an eval set so we get notified on semantic drift; the Console ties eval alerts to example traces so you can drill down to the root request.
[09:14] [28:32] Samir Patel: How does Request ID mapping work across retries? We saw duplicate IDs sometimes.
[09:40] Priya Desai: We append attempt metadata to the same root trace but create sub-spans for each retry attempt; the Console shows attempts grouped by root trace ID unless your client is issuing a new request id per retry. That mismatch is a common cause of split traces.
[09:58] Samir Patel: Oh interesting — so our client lib might need to pass 'x-redwood-root-id' to keep grouping.
[10:04] Priya Desai: Yes, we can share the SDK snippet. I'll add that to the action items.
[10:10] [31:00] Jordan Lee: Quick pricing note — if you need guaranteed residency and warmed models, Dedicated options have a monthly reserved cost plus usage. We'll send the pricing sheet.
[10:20] Emily Wong: Understood. Send the tier comparison and the SLA figures.
[10:24] Jordan Lee: Will do.
[10:26] [33:12] Priya Desai: One more tip: the Console has an index of 'error fingerprints' that clusters similar stack traces. Use it to find recurring failure patterns even if they cross different request IDs.
[10:40] Ruth Alvarez: That clustering would have been helpful in prior incidents. Can we export the cluster report?
[10:45] Priya Desai: Yes, exportable CSV with example traces, counts, and time buckets. We'll include an example in the pilot kit.
[10:53] [36:40] Marco Chen: On the architectural side, if you want stricter determinism, use strict variant pinning + explicit fallback routes that route to a compatibility shim rather than automatic quantized fallback. That reduces surprises but may increase error surface if the pinned variant is unavailable.
[11:05] Emily Wong: Sounds like a risk tradeoff — we'd prefer deterministic outputs over silent fallbacks.
[11:10] Priya Desai: Then we'll set the rollout to 'strict' in the pilot and add a fail-open policy only for canary traffic.
[11:16] [39:05] Samir Patel: For the pilot, what telemetry should we ship? Request logs, trace events, host metrics, and kube events?
[11:23] Priya Desai: Exactly those four. Plus optional prefix-hotset dumps if you want KV analytics. The SE will give you the forwarder config.
[11:30] Ruth Alvarez: We'll scope that with our infra team.
[11:34] [42:50] Priya Desai: Recap of remediation flow we demoed: identify failed trace -> open playback -> inspect kv flags + host metrics -> reproduce with exported payload -> adjust rollout/pinning or increase KV retention -> monitor via eval alerts.
[11:52] Jordan Lee: Excellent. Are there any other questions on the technical flow?
[11:57] Kenji Ito: One more compliance question — are audit logs tamper-evident? We need chain-of-custody for certain requests.
[12:05] Marco Chen: Audit trails are signed and stored with write-once options for Private deployments; for hosted we maintain tamper-evident logs with append-only storage and can provide attestation. We'll share specifics in the compliance packet.
[12:18] [48:00] Ruth Alvarez: Great. I think we have the info to move forward with the pilot. Timeline: we'd like to start next week.
[12:25] Jordan Lee: We'll aim to provision the pilot and send the starter kit. Priya — action items?
[12:31] Priya Desai: I'll prepare: (1) sample trace ingestion template, (2) SDK snippet for root-id, (3) export/debug tarball template, (4) pilot telemetry forwarder config.
[12:40] Jordan Lee: I'll send pricing and security pack. Ruth — can you send the 24-hour request log extract by Friday?
[12:46] Ruth Alvarez: Yes, I'll have my infra team push that. Samir will coordinate.
[12:50] Samir Patel: Yup.
[12:52] [52:10] Jordan Lee: Thank you everyone — we'll follow up with the calendar invite and next steps.
[12:56] Emily Wong: Thanks Jordan, Priya, Marco. Looking forward to the pilot.
[12:58] Priya Desai: Thanks all.
[13:00] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words misrecognized (e.g., 'quant' vs 'quantized', 'KV' as 'K V'). There is some crosstalk and brief pauses during screen-share.
